decks.title: Commercial Banks and the Central Bank — Part 1: Commercial Banks and Credit Creation
goals: Explain the primary and secondary functions of commercial banks, with types of deposits and loans
Calculate total deposits and credit created from an initial deposit and a reserve ratio
Explain the limitations of credit creation and the meaning of high-powered money

slides.heading: Commercial Banks and Credit Creation
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what **commercial banks** do, how they **create credit**, and what **limits** that power.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: deposits, loans, secondary services, credit creation, its limits, and high-powered money
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: When you put money in a bank, it does not simply sit in a vault. The bank lends most of it, and the loan soon comes back to some bank as a new deposit. In this part we see what commercial banks do for us, and how, together, they turn one deposit into many times as much.

slides.heading: What a commercial bank does
slides.body_md: Two **primary** functions define a bank; **secondary** functions add services.

nodes.label: Secondary: general utility (lockers, letters of credit, drafts)

visual.alt: Flow of commercial bank functions: primary functions of accepting deposits and advancing loans, and secondary functions of agency services and general utility services
visual.caption: Primary and secondary functions

slides.narration: Every commercial bank does two things above all: it accepts deposits and it advances loans. These are its primary functions. Around them it offers secondary services. Some are agency services, where it acts for a customer, like collecting cheques. Others are general utility services, like lockers and letters of credit.

slides.heading: Accepting deposits
slides.body_md: **Demand deposits** (current, savings) can be withdrawn any time; **time deposits** (recurring, fixed) are kept for a period and earn more.

rows: Any number of times, by cheque
Lump sums not needed for a while

visual.alt: Table of four kinds of bank deposits: current deposits allow unlimited withdrawals and usually pay no interest, suiting traders; savings deposits pay modest interest; recurring and fixed deposits are time deposits paying higher interest and withdrawn at maturity

slides.narration: Banks offer different deposits for different needs. A current account lets a trader pay and receive money many times a day, usually without interest. A savings account suits households and pays a little interest. Recurring and fixed deposits lock money in for a period, so the bank can lend it for longer and pays a higher rate.

slides.heading: Quick check: choosing a deposit
slides.body_md: A retired teacher wants the highest interest on a lump sum she will not need for three years. Which deposit suits her?
slides.narration: Think about how long she can leave the money untouched, and which deposit rewards that.

slides.heading: Advancing loans
slides.body_md: Banks lend through **cash credit**, **overdrafts**, **discounting bills** and **demand or term loans**.

rows: Draw up to a limit against security; interest on the amount used
Draw beyond the current-account balance up to a limit
Bank pays a bill now, less a discount, before it falls due
A lump sum repayable on demand or over a period

visual.alt: Table of forms of bank lending: cash credit up to a limit against security, overdrafts beyond the current-account balance, discounting bills of exchange before they fall due, and demand or term loans

slides.narration: The money deposited is lent out in several forms. Cash credit lets a firm draw up to a limit against security. An overdraft lets a current-account holder go beyond the balance. Discounting pays a trader the value of a bill before it falls due. Term loans finance machines and buildings. The interest earned is the bank's main income.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: three customers, three accounts
slides.body_md: Match an account to each imagined Lucknow customer.
bullets: A chemist paying and receiving many times a day: **current account**.
A student saving a little each month: **recurring deposit**.
A farmer needing money in two years: **fixed deposit**.
Rule: the more often money is needed, the more liquid the account.

rows: Any number of times, by cheque
Lump sums not needed for a while

visual.alt: Table of four kinds of bank deposits: current deposits allow unlimited withdrawals and usually pay no interest, suiting traders; savings deposits pay modest interest; recurring and fixed deposits are time deposits paying higher interest and withdrawn at maturity

slides.narration: Let us match accounts to people. The chemist makes many transactions daily, so only a current account will do. The student can put away a small fixed sum every month, which is what a recurring deposit is for. The farmer will not touch his money for two years, so a fixed deposit earns him the most.

slides.heading: Quick check: a kind of deposit
slides.body_md: Deposits that can be withdrawn at any time are called ___ deposits.
slides.narration: Current and savings deposits are payable whenever the depositor asks. What are they called?

slides.heading: Credit creation: the idea
slides.body_md: A bank keeps only a **reserve** (the **legal reserve ratio**) and lends the rest. The loan is spent and **redeposited**, so banks can lend again.

nodes.label: Seller deposits it in a bank

visual.alt: Flow of one round of credit creation: a new deposit, the bank keeps the required reserve and lends the rest, the loan is spent, and the seller deposits the money in a bank, starting the next round
visual.caption: One round of credit creation

slides.narration: Here is the key idea. Banks must keep only part of every deposit as a reserve. They lend the rest. The borrower spends the loan, and the seller deposits it in a bank. That bank keeps its reserve and lends again. Each round is smaller, but together they add up to many times the first deposit.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: Vasundhara Bank
slides.body_md: An imagined cooperative deposits **₹50,000**; reserve ratio **20 per cent**.
bullets: Round 1: keep 10,000, lend 40,000.
Round 2: deposit 40,000, keep 8,000, lend 32,000.

visual.alt: Table of deposit creation after an imagined deposit of 50,000 rupees with a 20 per cent reserve ratio: rounds of deposits 50,000, 40,000, 32,000, 25,600, with reserves of one-fifth and loans of four-fifths each time; all rounds together give deposits of 2,50,000, reserves of 50,000 and loans of 2,00,000
visual.caption: Imagined figures; totals by the formula.

slides.narration: A weavers' cooperative deposits fifty thousand rupees. The bank keeps ten thousand, one fifth, and lends forty thousand. That forty thousand returns as a deposit somewhere, and thirty-two thousand is lent. When all the rounds are done, total deposits reach two lakh fifty thousand, and the loans, the credit created, come to two lakh.

slides.narration: Each bar is one round. The pale top fifth of each bar is held back as a reserve, and the rest is lent and becomes the next, shorter bar. That is why the process cannot go on for ever: every round leaks one fifth into reserves, until the whole first deposit is held as reserves somewhere.

slides.heading: Quick check: total deposits
slides.body_md: A deposit of ₹50,000, a 20 per cent reserve ratio. Total deposits?
slides.narration: Divide the first deposit by the reserve ratio, written as a fraction.

slides.heading: The credit multiplier
slides.body_md: **Credit multiplier = 1 ÷ legal reserve ratio**. A **higher** ratio means a **smaller** multiplier.

visual.alt: Table of credit multipliers: reserve ratios of 10, 12.5, 20 and 25 per cent give multipliers of 10, 8, 5 and 4, and total deposits of 10,000, 8,000, 5,000 and 4,000 crore rupees from primary deposits of 1,000 crore
visual.caption: Multiplier = 1 ÷ reserve ratio.

slides.narration: The number of times deposits expand is the credit multiplier, one divided by the reserve ratio. With a ten per cent ratio the multiplier is ten; with twenty-five per cent it is only four. So when the central bank raises the reserve ratio, the banks' power to create credit shrinks.

visual.caption: Imagined economy: total deposits = primary deposits ÷ reserve ratio.

slides.narration: Here the same one thousand crore of primary deposits is run through four different reserve ratios. At ten per cent, banks can build deposits of ten thousand crore. At twelve and a half per cent, eight thousand. At twenty-five per cent, only four thousand. Raising the ratio is a powerful brake on credit.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the ratio is raised in Swarnapur
slides.body_md: Primary deposits **₹1,000 crore**; ratio raised from **10** to **12.5 per cent**.
bullets: Fall: ₹2,000 crore of deposits.

visual.alt: Table of credit multipliers: reserve ratios of 10, 12.5, 20 and 25 per cent give multipliers of 10, 8, 5 and 4, and total deposits of 10,000, 8,000, 5,000 and 4,000 crore rupees from primary deposits of 1,000 crore
visual.caption: Multiplier = 1 ÷ reserve ratio.

slides.narration: In the imagined Swarnapur economy, primary deposits are one thousand crore. With a ten per cent ratio, banks can build deposits of ten thousand crore. When the central bank raises the ratio to twelve and a half per cent, the total falls to eight thousand crore, two thousand crore less. That is how a ratio rise contracts credit.

slides.heading: Limits on credit creation
slides.body_md: The formula is a **maximum**. Real credit creation is smaller because of **cash drain**, lack of **willing borrowers** or **security**, and **central bank policy**.

rows: Part of every deposit must be held back
Cash kept by the public does not return as deposits
Banks can lend only if people want loans
Loans need sound security from borrowers
It can raise ratios or make credit dearer

visual.alt: Table of limits on credit creation: the legal reserve ratio, cash drain, the need for willing borrowers, the need for sound security, and central bank policy

slides.narration: In practice, banks create less than the formula says. People keep some cash at home, so it never returns as a deposit. Banks can lend only to people who want loans and can offer sound security. And the central bank can raise the reserve ratio at any time. Each of these limits shrinks the rounds.

slides.heading: High-powered money
slides.body_md: **High-powered money** = **currency held by the public** + **cash reserves of banks**. Deposits are built on it **many times over**.

rows: Cash reserves of banks (vault and central bank)

visual.alt: Table of high-powered money in an imagined economy: currency held by the public 640 crore plus cash reserves of banks 160 crore gives high-powered money of 800 crore rupees
visual.caption: Banks build deposits several times larger on this base.

slides.narration: All this credit rests on a base called high-powered money: the currency people hold plus the cash reserves of banks. It is called high-powered because banks build deposits several times larger on the reserves part. So when this base changes, the money supply changes by a multiple.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Currency with the public + bank reserves

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: primary and secondary functions of commercial banks, the credit multiplier, total deposits, credit created, and high-powered money

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Commercial banks accept deposits and advance loans, and add agency and utility services. Because they keep only a reserve and lend the rest, deposits expand by the credit multiplier, one over the reserve ratio. Leakages and policy keep actual credit below that maximum. High-powered money is the base on which it all rests.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the formula first: **total deposits = initial deposit ÷ reserve ratio**.
Credit created = total deposits **minus** the initial deposit.
In round tables, each new deposit equals the **previous loan**.
For limitations, name the **cash drain**, borrowers and security, and the reserve ratio.
High-powered money: **currency with the public + bank reserves**, not public deposits.

visual.alt: Table of deposit creation after an imagined deposit of 50,000 rupees with a 20 per cent reserve ratio: rounds of deposits 50,000, 40,000, 32,000, 25,600, with reserves of one-fifth and loans of four-fifths each time; all rounds together give deposits of 2,50,000, reserves of 50,000 and loans of 2,00,000
visual.caption: Imagined figures; totals by the formula.

slides.narration: Write the formula before you use it. Remember that credit created is total deposits minus the first deposit. In a table of rounds, every new deposit equals the loan of the round before. When asked about limits, give the cash drain, borrowers and security, and the reserve ratio. And define high-powered money correctly.

decks.title: Commercial Banks and the Central Bank — Part 2: The Reserve Bank and Credit Control
goals: Explain the functions of the Reserve Bank of India
Explain how each quantitative instrument changes the flow of credit, and recommend its direction
Distinguish quantitative from qualitative methods and explain the qualitative tools

slides.heading: The Reserve Bank and Credit Control
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the **Reserve Bank of India**, its **functions**, and the **quantitative** and **qualitative** tools it uses to control credit.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: functions of the Reserve Bank, its role as lender of last resort, quantitative and qualitative tools, and choosing between them
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Commercial banks create credit, but someone must keep that power in check. In India that is the Reserve Bank, set up in nineteen thirty-five and nationalised in nineteen forty-nine. In this part we see what it does, and how it uses its tools to expand or contract credit.

slides.heading: Functions of the Reserve Bank

rows: Sole issuer of currency notes, except one-rupee notes
Keeps its accounts, makes payments, manages its debt
Holds banks' reserves, clears their claims, supervises them
Lends to sound banks in a crisis
Holds foreign currencies and gold; steadies the rupee

visual.alt: Table of the functions of the Reserve Bank of India: bank of issue, banker to the government, bankers' bank, lender of last resort, custodian of foreign exchange reserves, and controller of credit
visual.caption: Set up in 1935; nationalised in 1949.

slides.narration: The Reserve Bank issues all currency notes except the one-rupee note. It is banker to the government and to the banks. It lends to banks in a crisis, holds the country's foreign exchange reserves, and controls credit. Unlike a commercial bank, it does not work for profit but for stable prices and a stable banking system.

slides.heading: Banker to the government and to banks
slides.body_md: It keeps the **government's accounts** and **manages its debt**; it holds **banks' reserves**, **clears** their claims and **supervises** them.

visual.alt: Table comparing a commercial bank and the Reserve Bank of India: aim, whom they deal with, currency issue and their relation to credit

slides.narration: For the government, the Reserve Bank keeps accounts, makes payments and arranges borrowing by selling bonds. For banks, it does what banks do for us: it holds their reserves, settles what they owe one another, and lends to them. That is why it is called the bankers' bank.

slides.heading: Lender of last resort
slides.body_md: When a **sound bank** cannot get cash anywhere else, the central bank **lends to it**, so a panic does not spread.

nodes.label: Rumour causes a rush to withdraw
Sound bank runs short of cash

visual.alt: Flow of the lender of last resort role: a rumour causes a rush to withdraw, a sound bank runs short of cash, no other lender helps, the central bank lends against securities, depositors are paid and the panic stops
visual.caption: Lender of last resort

slides.narration: Imagine a false rumour sends depositors rushing to a sound bank. It cannot sell its loans quickly, and other lenders hold back. The Reserve Bank lends to it against securities, depositors are paid, and confidence returns. This role as lender of last resort protects the whole banking system.

slides.heading: Quick check: which function?
slides.body_md: A sound bank facing a rush of withdrawals borrows from the RBI. Which function is at work?
slides.narration: Who does a bank turn to when no one else will lend?

slides.heading: Quantitative tools: rates
slides.body_md: **Repo rate**: short-term loans to banks against securities. **Reverse repo**: what the central bank pays on banks' surplus funds. **Bank rate**: longer-term lending or rediscounting.

rows: Rate for short-term loans to banks against securities
Rate the central bank pays on banks' surplus funds
Rate for longer-term lending or rediscounting
Share of deposits kept as cash with the central bank
Share of deposits kept by banks in liquid assets
Sale or purchase of government securities

visual.alt: Table of quantitative instruments: repo rate, reverse repo rate, bank rate, cash reserve ratio, statutory liquidity ratio and open market operations, with the direction of change against inflation (raise, or sell securities) and against deficient demand (cut, or buy securities)
visual.caption: Directions only; no current values are stated.

slides.narration: Quantitative tools change the total volume and cost of credit. The repo rate is what banks pay for short-term funds from the central bank against government securities. The reverse repo rate is what the central bank pays when banks park surplus funds with it. The bank rate applies to longer-term lending. Raising any of them makes credit dearer.

slides.heading: How a repo rate rise works

visual.alt: Flow of a repo rate rise: banks pay more for funds, raise their loan rates, households and firms borrow and spend less, and the pressure on prices eases
visual.caption: How a repo rise works

slides.narration: Follow a rise in the repo rate. Banks now pay more for funds, so they charge more on their own loans. Households and firms borrow less, so they spend less on homes, cars and machines. With lower demand, the pressure on prices eases. A cut works the other way, encouraging borrowing and spending.

slides.heading: Quantitative tools: reserve ratios
slides.body_md: **CRR**: share of deposits kept as **cash with the central bank**. **SLR**: share kept by the bank **itself** in **liquid assets**. Raising either leaves **less to lend**.

slides.narration: Two ratios lock up part of every deposit. The cash reserve ratio is kept as cash with the central bank. The statutory liquidity ratio is kept by the bank itself in cash, gold and approved government securities. Here, with imagined ratios, an imagined bank with six hundred crore of deposits can lend only four hundred and fifty crore.

slides.narration: Let us compute. Five per cent of six hundred crore is thirty crore, kept as cash with the central bank. Twenty per cent is one hundred and twenty crore, held in liquid assets. What remains, four hundred and fifty crore, is what the bank can lend. Raise either ratio and that figure falls.

slides.narration: Subtract both required holdings from total deposits.

slides.heading: Open market operations
slides.body_md: **Selling** securities **drains** bank reserves; **buying** them **adds** reserves.

visual.alt: Flow of an open market sale: buyers pay from their bank deposits, bank reserves fall, and banks lend less
visual.caption: Open market sale

slides.narration: In open market operations the central bank buys or sells government securities. When it sells, buyers pay out of their bank deposits, so banks lose reserves and must lend less. When it buys, it pays money into the banking system, reserves rise and banks can lend more.

slides.heading: Qualitative (selective) tools
slides.body_md: They steer the **direction** of credit: **margin requirements**, **credit rationing**, **moral suasion**, **direct action**.

rows: A higher margin means a smaller loan against the same security
Ceilings or quotas on credit for certain purposes
Advice and persuasion of banks, without legal force
Penalties or denial of facilities to banks that ignore directions

visual.alt: Table of qualitative credit tools: margin requirements, credit rationing, moral suasion and direct action, with how each works

slides.narration: Sometimes the problem is not the total amount of credit but where it goes, for example into hoarding gold or land. Then the central bank uses selective tools. It can raise margins on loans against those goods, set ceilings on such loans, persuade banks to go slow, or take direct action against banks that ignore it.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a higher margin on pulses
slides.body_md: An imagined trader offers pulses worth **₹10 lakh** as security.
bullets: Margin 30 per cent: loan = 70 per cent = **₹7 lakh**.
Margin 50 per cent: loan = 50 per cent = **₹5 lakh**.
Less credit for hoarding pulses; other borrowers are not touched.

visual.alt: Table showing that a trader offering pulses worth 10 lakh rupees can borrow 7 lakh with a 30 per cent margin but only 5 lakh with a 50 per cent margin
visual.caption: Imagined figures.

slides.narration: Here is how a margin works. With a thirty per cent margin, a trader can borrow seventy per cent of the value of his pulses, seven lakh rupees. If the central bank raises the margin to fifty per cent, he can borrow only five lakh. Hoarding with borrowed money becomes harder, while credit for everyone else is unchanged.

slides.body_md: The governor meets bank heads and urges them, without any order, to slow loans for land. This is…
slides.narration: Is there a legal order here, or only persuasion?

slides.heading: Quantitative or qualitative?
columns:
**Quantitative**

- Control the **total volume and cost** of credit.
- Affect **all** borrowers.
- Repo, reverse repo, bank rate, CRR, SLR, open market operations.

**Qualitative**

- Control the **direction** of credit.
- Aim at **particular uses**.
- Margins, rationing, moral suasion, direct action.

rows: Total volume and cost of credit
Repo, CRR, SLR, open market operations
Margins, rationing, moral suasion, direct action

visual.alt: Table comparing quantitative and qualitative methods of credit control: volume against direction, all borrowers against particular uses, and examples of each

slides.narration: Use quantitative tools when the whole economy has too much or too little spending, because they change credit for everyone. Use qualitative tools when the trouble is confined to a few goods or sectors, because they target credit for those uses only. Often the two are used together.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

Repo, reverse repo, bank rate, CRR, SLR, open market operations

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: functions of the Reserve Bank, quantitative tools, the direction against inflation, qualitative tools, and when to use each kind

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. The Reserve Bank issues currency, serves the government and the banks, rescues sound banks in a crisis and holds foreign exchange. It controls credit with quantitative tools that change its volume and cost, and with qualitative tools that change its direction. Against inflation, rates and ratios go up and securities are sold.

sections.heading: 4. The Reserve Bank of India: functions
sections.body_md:
- Set up in **1935** (under the RBI Act, 1934); **nationalised in 1949**.
- **Bank of issue**: sole issuer of currency notes except one-rupee notes (issued, like coins, by the Government of India).
- **Banker, agent and adviser to the government**: accounts, payments, management of public debt.
- **Bankers' bank and supervisor**: holds reserves, clears claims, regulates banks.
- **Lender of last resort**: lends to sound banks in a crisis.
- **Custodian of foreign exchange reserves** and **controller of credit**.

key_terms.definition_md: The central bank's role of lending to banks when no other source of funds is available.
The authority with the sole right to issue currency notes.

rows: Sole issuer of currency notes, except one-rupee notes

sections.heading: 5. Quantitative credit control
sections.body_md:
- **Repo rate**: rate at which the central bank lends short-term to banks against government securities (a repurchase agreement). **Reverse repo rate**: rate it pays when banks park surplus funds with it. **Bank rate**: rate for longer-term lending or rediscounting bills.
- **CRR**: share of deposits held as **cash with the central bank**. **SLR**: share held by banks **themselves** in cash, gold and approved securities.
- **Open market operations**: selling securities drains reserves; buying adds them.
- Against **inflation**: raise rates and ratios, sell securities. Against **deficient demand**: the reverse.
- Imagined bank: deposits 600, CRR 5 per cent, SLR 20 per cent: lendable **450** crore.

sections.heading: 6. Qualitative (selective) credit control
sections.body_md:
- **Margin requirements**: raising the margin reduces the loan available against a security.
- **Credit rationing**: ceilings or quotas on credit for particular purposes.
- **Moral suasion**: persuasion and advice to banks, without legal force.
- **Direct action**: penalties or denial of facilities for banks that ignore directions.
- **Quantitative vs qualitative**: volume and cost for all borrowers versus direction and use for particular purposes; selective tools suit price rises in a **few commodities**, but can be **evaded**.

questions.stem_md: A banking manual for new clerks at an imagined Nashik bank lists its two primary functions. They are

options.text_md: issuing currency notes and keeping foreign exchange
accepting deposits and advancing loans
renting lockers and selling traveller's cheques
collecting cheques and paying insurance premiums

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** accepting deposits and advancing loans. Accepting deposits and advancing loans are the core (primary) functions of every commercial bank. Issuing notes is a central-bank function; lockers, cheque collection and premium payments are secondary (utility or agency) functions.

questions.stem_md: Meera, a retired teacher in an imagined Mysuru suburb, wants to place a lump sum with a bank for three years at the highest interest and does not need to withdraw it before then. Which deposit suits her?

options.text_md: A current account
A savings account
A locker
A fixed (time) deposit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A fixed (time) deposit. A fixed deposit is kept for a stated period and earns a higher rate because the bank can lend it for that period. A current account pays no interest, a savings account pays less, and a locker earns nothing.

questions.stem_md: A cloth merchant in an imagined Erode market writes cheques for more than the balance in his current account, up to a limit agreed with his bank, and pays interest only on the extra amount. This form of lending is

options.text_md: an overdraft
a fixed deposit
a demand draft
a recurring deposit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** an overdraft. An overdraft lets a current-account holder draw beyond the balance up to a limit, with interest charged only on the amount overdrawn. The other options are deposits or a payment instrument, not loans.

questions.stem_md: A spice exporter in an imagined Kochi firm holds a buyer's bill payable in 90 days but needs cash today. The bank pays him the bill's value minus a small charge now. The bank is

options.text_md: collecting a cheque as an agent
giving a term loan for ten years
discounting a bill of exchange
accepting a recurring deposit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** discounting a bill of exchange. Paying the present value of a bill before it is due, less a discount, is discounting a bill of exchange, a way of advancing short-term credit.

questions.stem_md: On a standing instruction from Arjun, an imagined Guwahati depositor, his bank pays his life-insurance premium and his electricity bill from his account every month. This is an example of

options.text_md: a primary function of a commercial bank
a function of the central bank
an agency function of a commercial bank
credit creation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** an agency function of a commercial bank. Making payments on a customer's behalf is an agency function: the bank acts as the customer's agent. It is not one of the two primary functions.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A wholesale trader who makes many payments every day is better served by a current account than by a savings account.

**Reason (R):** A current account allows any number of deposits and withdrawals in a day, although it usually pays no interest.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: a trader needs unlimited transactions, which a current account allows; giving up interest is the price of that freedom.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A savings account at an imagined Ajmer bank earns some interest but may limit how often money is withdrawn.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. A savings account encourages saving: it pays a modest interest rate and may limit the number of withdrawals in a period.

questions.stem_md: Deposits that can be withdrawn by cheque or on demand at any time, such as current and savings deposits, are called ___ deposits.
questions.solution_md: Current and savings deposits are demand deposits, payable whenever the depositor asks; fixed deposits are time deposits.

questions.stem_md: Match each service that an imagined Bhubaneswar branch provides with the kind of bank function it belongs to.

options.text_md: Giving a cash-credit limit to a rice mill
Opening a recurring deposit for a student
Collecting a dividend warrant for a shareholder
Renting out a safe-deposit locker

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Cash credit is a loan and a recurring deposit is a deposit (both primary). Collecting dividends acts on the customer's behalf (agency). A locker is a general utility service.

questions.stem_md: Explain the two primary functions of a commercial bank, giving one type under each, for a leaflet of an imagined rural bank in Bastar.
questions.solution_md: Two primary functions, each with one type.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Accepting deposits**: the bank takes people's savings in **current, savings, recurring or fixed deposits**, for example a farmer's fixed deposit.
2. **Advancing loans**: it lends these funds as **cash credit, overdrafts, term loans** or by discounting bills, for example a crop loan.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the agency functions and the general utility functions of an imagined Raipur commercial bank, with one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Acting for the customer versus general services.

answer.model_answer_md: **Agency functions**: the bank acts **on behalf of a customer**, for example **collecting cheques** or paying insurance premiums from the customer's account. **General utility functions**: services offered to the **public at large** whether or not the bank acts as agent, for example **lockers** or issuing letters of credit.

questions.stem_md: Explain three forms in which a commercial bank in an imagined Jalandhar market advances loans to its customers.
questions.solution_md: Any three forms: cash credit, overdraft, discounting, demand or term loans.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Cash credit**: the borrower may draw up to a limit against goods or other security, paying interest only on the amount used.
2. **Overdraft**: a current-account holder draws more than the balance, up to an agreed limit.
3. **Discounting bills of exchange**: the bank pays a bill's value before it falls due, keeping a small discount (also **term loans** for buying machines).

questions.stem_md: Recommend a suitable deposit account for each of three imagined customers of a Lucknow bank, with a reason: (a) a chemist who receives and pays money many times a day, (b) a college student saving a little from her stipend each month, (c) a farmer who has sold his crop and will need the money for a wedding in two years.
questions.solution_md: Match the account to how often money is needed.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Current account**: it allows **unlimited transactions**, which a busy chemist needs.
(b) **Recurring deposit** (or savings account): she deposits **a fixed sum every month** and earns interest.
(c) **Fixed deposit for two years**: the money is not needed before then, so it earns a **higher rate**.

marking_scheme.step: Recurring or savings deposit with reason

questions.stem_md:
A new branch of an imagined cooperative bank is opening in a town near Bhilwara.

(a) Explain the two primary functions it will perform, naming the types of deposits and loans. [3]
(b) Explain two secondary functions it could offer local traders. [2]
questions.solution_md: Deposits and loans with types; one agency and one utility function.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Accepting deposits**: it will open **current accounts** for traders (unlimited transactions, no interest), **savings accounts** for households (some interest), and **fixed and recurring deposits** for longer-term savers (higher interest). **Advancing loans**: it will lend these funds as **cash credit** and **overdrafts** for working capital, **discount bills** of exchange, and give **term loans** for machines or shops. The difference between the interest it earns and pays is its main income.
(b) **Agency**: **collecting cheques and bills** and making payments such as taxes or premiums for customers. **General utility**: **lockers**, **letters of credit** and drafts for traders who buy from distant suppliers.

questions.stem_md: The imagined banks of the Swarnapur economy must keep 12.5 per cent of their deposits as reserves. What is the credit multiplier?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 8. Credit multiplier = 1 ÷ legal reserve ratio = 1 ÷ 0.125 = 8.

questions.stem_md: Banks in the imagined Kosi Valley receive a fresh deposit of ₹80 crore and must keep 25 per cent as reserves. If the process is completed with no cash leaking out, total deposits become

options.text_md: ₹240 crore
₹160 crore
₹20 crore
₹320 crore

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹320 crore. Total deposits = 80 ÷ 0.25 = 320. ₹240 crore is the credit (loans) created, total deposits minus the initial deposit.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Reserve Bank training slide defines high-powered money. It consists of

options.text_md: demand deposits plus time deposits of the public
currency held by the public plus the cash reserves of banks
gold held by the central bank only
loans given by commercial banks

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** currency held by the public plus the cash reserves of banks. High-powered (reserve) money is currency with the public plus banks' cash reserves (in their vaults and with the central bank). Deposits and loans are created on top of it.

questions.stem_md: Borrowers from imagined banks in a Bundelkhand district keep a large part of their loans as cash at home instead of depositing it. What happens to credit creation?

options.text_md: It is smaller than the simple formula suggests, because the cash does not return to banks as new deposits
It is larger than the formula, because people hold more money
It is unchanged, because the reserve ratio is unchanged
It stops completely after the first loan

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It is smaller than the simple formula suggests, because the cash does not return to banks as new deposits. Each round of new deposits depends on loans coming back into banks. Cash kept at home is a leakage, so later rounds are smaller and total credit falls short of 1 ÷ LRR times the deposit.

questions.stem_md: The central bank of the imagined Swarnapur economy raises the reserve ratio from 10 to 12.5 per cent. With primary deposits of ₹1000 crore, total deposits that banks can create

options.text_md: rise from ₹8,000 crore to ₹10,000 crore
fall from ₹10,000 crore to ₹8,000 crore
stay the same
fall to ₹1000 crore

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** fall from ₹10,000 crore to ₹8,000 crore. Before: 1000 ÷ 0.1 = 10,000. After: 1000 ÷ 0.125 = 8,000. A higher reserve ratio lowers the multiplier from 10 to 8.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When people withdraw part of their loans in cash and keep it, banks create less credit than the multiplier formula shows.

**Reason (R):** Cash held by the public does not come back to the banks as fresh deposits that can be lent again.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: credit creation depends on every loan returning as a new deposit; cash kept outside the banks breaks the chain.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** High-powered money is so called because a given amount of it can support a much larger amount of bank deposits.

**Reason (R):** High-powered money is made up mainly of the demand deposits of the public with commercial banks.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: banks build deposits several times larger on the base of reserves. R is false: high-powered money is currency with the public plus bank reserves; the public's demand deposits are created on top of it.

questions.stem_md: True or false? An imagined bank in Shimla can create an unlimited amount of credit from a single deposit, because every loan returns to it as a new deposit.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. The legal reserve ratio means part of each deposit must be held back, so the rounds shrink; credit is limited to (1 ÷ LRR − 1) times the deposit, and cash leakages and a shortage of willing borrowers cut it further.

questions.stem_md: In the simple model of credit creation, the credit multiplier of a banking system equals one divided by the legal ___ ratio.
questions.solution_md: Credit multiplier = 1 ÷ legal reserve ratio (the share of deposits banks must keep as reserves).

questions.stem_md: An imagined weavers' cooperative deposits ₹50,000 in Vasundhara Bank, and all banks must keep 20 per cent of deposits as reserves. Find the total deposits created when the process is complete (in ₹), assuming no cash leaves the banks.
With the same imagined deposit of ₹50,000 at Vasundhara Bank and a 20 per cent reserve ratio, how much credit (total loans) does the banking system create (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md: Total deposits ₹2,50,000 − initial deposit ₹50,000 = 200000, that is ₹2,00,000.

questions.stem_md: The imagined banks of a hill district want total deposits of ₹4,00,000, and the reserve ratio is 12.5 per cent. What initial deposit is needed (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md: Multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.125 = 8; initial deposit = 4,00,000 ÷ 8 = 50000, that is ₹50,000.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined economy, currency held by the public is ₹640 crore and the cash reserves of banks (in their vaults and with the central bank) are ₹160 crore. Find its high-powered money (in ₹ crore).
questions.solution_md: High-powered money = currency with the public + bank reserves = 640 + 160 = 800.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps by which a deposit made in the imagined Vasundhara Bank leads to a fresh deposit in another bank.

options.text_md: The supplier deposits the money in his own bank, which can lend again
The cooperative deposits its money in Vasundhara Bank
The borrower pays a supplier with the loan
The bank keeps the required reserve and lends the rest

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). Deposit, then reserve and loan, then spending of the loan, then a new deposit elsewhere: one round of credit creation.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: What is high-powered money? Explain why an imagined central bank economist calls it "high-powered".
questions.solution_md: Components and the multiple-expansion reason.

answer.model_answer_md: **High-powered money** (reserve money) is the **currency held by the public plus the cash reserves of banks**. It is "high-powered" because banks can build **deposits several times larger** on these reserves through credit creation, so a change in it changes the money supply **by a multiple**.

questions.stem_md: State two limitations on the power of the imagined banks of a tribal district in Jharkhand to create credit.
questions.solution_md: Any two: reserve ratio, cash drain, borrowers, security, banking habit, central-bank policy.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Cash drain**: borrowers there keep much of their money as **cash**, so it does not return as deposits.
2. **Few willing borrowers or little security**: banks can lend only to people who **want loans** and can offer **acceptable security** (also the reserve ratio set by the central bank).

questions.stem_md: An imagined weavers' cooperative deposits ₹50,000 in Vasundhara Bank; the reserve ratio is 20 per cent. Show the first three rounds of deposits, reserves and loans, and find the total deposits created.
questions.solution_md: Reserve 20 per cent, lend 80 per cent, repeat; total by the multiplier.

answer.model_answer_md: **Round 1:** deposit 50,000, reserve **10,000**, loan **40,000**. **Round 2:** the loan returns as a deposit of 40,000; reserve 8,000, loan **32,000**. **Round 3:** deposit 32,000; reserve 6,400, loan **25,600**. When the rounds are complete, total deposits = 50,000 × 1 ÷ 0.2 = **₹2,50,000**.

questions.stem_md: Primary deposits in the imagined Swarnapur economy are ₹1000 crore. Its central bank raises the reserve ratio from 10 to 12.5 per cent. Calculate total deposits before and after, and explain the effect on credit.
questions.solution_md: Compute both totals; explain the smaller multiplier.

answer.model_answer_md: **Before:** multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10; total deposits = **₹10,000 crore**. **After:** multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.125 = 8; total deposits = **₹8,000 crore**. Deposits fall by **₹2,000 crore**: banks must hold back more of each deposit, so **less is lent** in every round and total credit **contracts**, which suits a time of excess demand.

questions.stem_md:
Bank deposits in the imagined town of Rampur are all held in banks that keep 20 per cent as reserves.

(a) A cooperative deposits ₹50,000. Explain the process of credit creation round by round and find the total deposits and credit created. [3]
(b) State two assumptions of this process. [2]
questions.solution_md: Rounds; totals; two assumptions.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The bank keeps **₹10,000** (20 per cent) and lends **₹40,000**. The borrower pays a supplier, who **deposits** it in a bank: a new deposit of 40,000, of which 32,000 is lent. Next, 32,000 is deposited and 25,600 lent, and so on, each round smaller. Total deposits = 50,000 × 1 ÷ 0.2 = **₹2,50,000**; credit created = 2,50,000 − 50,000 = **₹2,00,000**.
(b) 1. **All loans return** to the banks as deposits: no cash is kept outside. 2. Banks keep **only the required reserve** and lend all the rest, and there are enough **willing borrowers**.

questions.stem_md:
A student in an imagined Jabalpur school says, "Banks can create as much money as they like, because every loan comes back as a deposit."

(a) Explain what is correct in her statement. [2]
(b) Evaluate it by explaining three limitations on credit creation. [3]
questions.solution_md: What holds, then three limits and a verdict.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) She is right that **loans create deposits**: money lent is spent and **redeposited**, so banks can lend again and total deposits become **a multiple** of the first deposit.
(b) But the multiple is **limited**. 1. **Legal reserve ratio**: part of every deposit must be kept as reserves, so the rounds **shrink**, and the total is capped at 1 ÷ LRR times the deposit. 2. **Cash drain**: people keep some money as **cash**, which does not return, so actual credit is smaller still. 3. **Borrowers and security**: banks lend only to those who **want loans** and offer **sound security**; in a slump, demand for loans is weak. The central bank can also tighten the ratio. So banks cannot create credit **without limit**.

questions.stem_md: A coin collector in an imagined Pune club notes who issues India's money. Currency notes of every denomination except the one-rupee note are issued by

options.text_md: the Ministry of Finance
the State Bank of India
the Reserve Bank of India
every commercial bank

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the Reserve Bank of India. The RBI has the sole right to issue currency notes, except one-rupee notes, which (like coins) are issued by the Government of India.

questions.stem_md: Depositors rush to withdraw cash from an imagined but sound commercial bank in Indore after a false rumour. The bank borrows from the RBI to meet the withdrawals. Which function of the RBI is at work?

options.text_md: Custodian of foreign exchange reserves
Controller of credit through moral suasion
Bank of issue
Lender of last resort

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Lender of last resort. When a bank cannot get funds anywhere else, the central bank lends to it, which prevents a panic from spreading. This is its role as lender of last resort.

questions.stem_md: The RBI keeps the central government's accounts, makes its payments and arranges its borrowing by selling its bonds. Which role is this, according to an imagined Delhi civil-services handbook?

options.text_md: Banker's bank
Lender of last resort
Clearing house for commercial banks
Banker, agent and adviser to the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Banker, agent and adviser to the government. Holding the government's accounts, handling its payments and managing its borrowing are the functions of a banker and agent to the government.

questions.stem_md: The RBI holds the country's reserves of foreign currencies and gold and uses them to steady the rupee when needed. In this role it acts as

options.text_md: banker to the government
bank of issue
custodian of foreign exchange reserves
clearing house

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** custodian of foreign exchange reserves. Keeping and managing the country's foreign currency and gold reserves is the custodian role.

questions.stem_md: A timeline in an imagined school exhibition on Indian banking marks two dates for the RBI. Which pair is correct?

options.text_md: Set up in 1947; nationalised in 1969
Set up in 1935; nationalised in 1949
Set up in 1921; nationalised in 1955
Set up in 1949; nationalised in 1980

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Set up in 1935; nationalised in 1949. The RBI began work in 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934, and was nationalised in 1949. (Many commercial banks were nationalised in 1969 and 1980.)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Unlike a commercial bank, the RBI does not aim to maximise its profit.

**Reason (R):** As the central bank, the RBI acts in the public interest, for example to keep prices and the banking system stable.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: a central bank's aims are monetary and financial stability, not profit for its owners.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A display at an imagined Chennai banking museum states that the Reserve Bank of India has been owned by the Government of India since its nationalisation in 1949.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The RBI was nationalised in 1949 and has been fully government-owned since then.

questions.stem_md: Explain the role of the RBI as lender of last resort, using an imagined bank in Agra that faces a sudden rush of withdrawals.
questions.solution_md: Last source of funds; prevents collapse and panic.

answer.model_answer_md: When the Agra bank's **cash runs short** and **no one else will lend** to it, the RBI **lends to it** against eligible securities. Depositors are paid, **panic does not spread** to other banks, and the **banking system stays stable**.

marking_scheme.step: RBI lends when no other source exists

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which the RBI acts as banker to the government, as an imagined Finance Ministry trainee would describe them.
questions.solution_md: Accounts and payments; public debt or advances or advice.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It **keeps the government's accounts**, receiving its revenue and **making its payments**.
2. It **manages public debt**: it sells government bonds and pays interest on them (and gives short-term advances to cover temporary gaps, besides advising on monetary matters).

questions.stem_md: Explain three ways in which the RBI acts as a "bankers' bank" for the imagined commercial banks of a state like Karnataka.
questions.solution_md: Reserves, clearing, lending or supervision.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Keeps their cash reserves**: banks must hold part of their deposits (the CRR) with the RBI.
2. **Clearing**: banks settle what they owe one another through their **accounts with the RBI**.
3. **Lends to them**, by rediscounting bills or giving loans against securities, and as **lender of last resort** in a crisis (it also supervises them).

questions.stem_md: Give three differences between an imagined commercial bank in Surat and the Reserve Bank of India.
questions.solution_md: Aim, customers, powers.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Aim**: the commercial bank works for **profit**; the RBI works for **monetary and financial stability**.
2. **Customers**: the commercial bank deals with the **public**; the RBI deals with **banks and the government**.
3. **Powers**: the commercial bank **cannot issue notes** and must obey reserve rules; the RBI **issues currency** and **controls credit**.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined exhibition panel in a Kolkata museum is titled "What the Reserve Bank does".

(a) Explain three of its functions as a bank of issue and a bank to banks. [3]
(b) Explain two of its other functions. [2]
questions.solution_md: Issue, bankers' bank, last resort; two other functions.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) 1. **Bank of issue**: it has the **sole right to issue currency notes** (except one-rupee notes), which keeps the currency uniform and trusted. 2. **Bankers' bank**: banks keep **reserves** with it and **settle claims** on one another through it. 3. **Lender of last resort**: it **lends to banks in trouble**, which prevents panics.
(b) 1. **Banker to the government**: it keeps government accounts, makes payments and **manages public debt**. 2. **Custodian of foreign exchange reserves**: it holds foreign currencies and gold and uses them to **steady the rupee** (it is also the **controller of credit**).

marking_scheme.step: Custodian of reserves or credit control

questions.stem_md: In the imagined Swarnapur economy, the repo rate is the rate at which

options.text_md: the central bank lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities
commercial banks lend to farmers
commercial banks lend to one another overnight without security
the government borrows from the public

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the central bank lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities. Repo is a repurchase agreement: the central bank lends short-term to banks against government securities, which the banks buy back. The reverse repo is the rate at which the central bank borrows from banks.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Swarnapur Central Bank raises its reverse repo rate while leaving other rates unchanged. The most likely effect is that commercial banks

options.text_md: borrow more from the central bank
park more surplus funds with the central bank and lend less to the public
lend more to the public at lower rates
cut the interest they pay on fixed deposits

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** park more surplus funds with the central bank and lend less to the public. A higher reverse repo rate makes it more rewarding for banks to keep surplus funds with the central bank, so less is lent to the public: credit contracts.

questions.stem_md: A trainee at an imagined Chandigarh bank asks how the statutory liquidity ratio differs from the cash reserve ratio. Under the SLR, a bank must keep a share of its deposits

options.text_md: as cash with the central bank only
as loans to small industries
with foreign banks
with itself, in liquid assets such as cash, gold and approved government securities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** with itself, in liquid assets such as cash, gold and approved government securities. The SLR is kept by the bank itself in liquid assets (cash, gold, approved securities). The CRR is the share kept as cash with the central bank.

questions.stem_md: Output is falling in an imagined economy and its central bank cuts the cash reserve ratio. Why should this help?

options.text_md: Banks need to keep less cash with the central bank, so they can lend more
Banks must keep more cash idle, so they lend less
It raises taxes on bank deposits
It makes government bonds more expensive for banks to buy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Banks need to keep less cash with the central bank, so they can lend more. A lower CRR frees part of banks' deposits for lending; more credit raises spending and output.

questions.stem_md: Prices in the imagined Swarnapur economy are rising because of excess demand. Which combination of quantitative steps by its central bank suits the situation?

options.text_md: Cut the repo rate, cut the CRR and buy government securities
Raise the repo rate but buy government securities
Raise the repo rate, raise the CRR and sell government securities
Cut the bank rate and raise the reverse repo rate

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Raise the repo rate, raise the CRR and sell government securities. All three steps in the first option make credit dearer or scarcer, which reduces spending. The second option expands credit; the others mix opposite directions.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Mumbai finance newsletter explains the bank rate. It is the rate at which the central bank

options.text_md: pays interest on savings accounts
buys foreign currency
lends to commercial banks for longer periods or rediscounts their bills, without a repurchase agreement
lends overnight to the government only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** lends to commercial banks for longer periods or rediscounts their bills, without a repurchase agreement. The bank rate is the standard rate for the central bank's longer-term lending to banks (or rediscounting their bills); unlike the repo, there is no repurchase agreement.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Raising either the CRR or the SLR reduces the funds that commercial banks can lend.

**Reason (R):** Under both the CRR and the SLR, banks must keep the required reserves as cash with the central bank.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: both lock up part of deposits. R is false: only CRR reserves are held with the central bank; SLR assets are kept by the banks themselves in cash, gold and approved securities.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When the central bank buys government securities in the open market, the lending capacity of banks rises.

**Reason (R):** The central bank pays for the securities, so cash reserves flow into the banking system.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: payment for the securities adds to banks' reserves, which they can lend several times over.

questions.stem_md: An imagined bank in Vadodara has deposits of ₹600 crore. Suppose (imagined ratios) it must keep 5 per cent as CRR with the central bank and 20 per cent in SLR assets. How much can it lend (in ₹ crore)?
Match each step taken by the imagined Swarnapur Central Bank with the instrument of credit control it uses.

options.text_md: It sells treasury bonds to banks and the public
It asks banks to keep a bigger share of deposits as cash with it
It charges banks more for overnight funds against securities
It raises the share of deposits banks must hold in approved securities

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Selling bonds is an open market operation; cash with the central bank is the CRR; overnight funds against securities are repo; holding approved securities is the SLR.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the cash reserve ratio and the statutory liquidity ratio, as an imagined bank's treasury officer in Hyderabad would explain them.
questions.solution_md: Where and in what form the reserve is kept.

answer.model_answer_md: **CRR**: the share of deposits a bank must keep **as cash with the central bank**; it earns nothing. **SLR**: the share of deposits a bank must keep **with itself in liquid assets** such as cash, gold and **approved government securities**, which may earn interest.

marking_scheme.step: CRR: cash with the central bank
SLR: liquid assets kept by the bank

questions.stem_md: Demand is deficient in an imagined economy. Should its central bank buy or sell securities in the open market? Explain.
questions.solution_md: Buy: reserves up, credit up.

answer.model_answer_md: It should **buy securities**. It pays for them, so **cash reserves of banks rise**; banks can **lend more**, credit becomes easier, and **spending and output rise**.

questions.stem_md: Prices in the imagined Swarnapur economy have risen for several months because spending exceeds what can be produced. Recommend three quantitative measures to its central bank, with the direction of each and how it works.
questions.solution_md: Three contractionary quantitative tools with mechanism.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Raise the repo rate** (and bank rate): banks pay more for funds, so they **charge more on loans** and borrowing falls.
2. **Raise the CRR** (or SLR): more of each deposit is locked up, so banks have **less to lend**.
3. **Sell government securities** (open market operations): buyers pay with bank money, so **bank reserves fall** and credit contracts.

marking_scheme.step: Repo or bank rate raised, with mechanism
CRR or SLR raised, with mechanism

questions.stem_md: The central bank of an imagined economy raises its bank rate. Trace the effect, step by step, on the loans of commercial banks, on spending and on prices.
questions.solution_md: Cost of funds, borrowing, demand, prices.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Banks now pay **more** when they borrow from or rediscount bills with the central bank, so they **raise their own lending rates**.
2. Dearer loans make firms and households **borrow less**, so **investment and consumer spending fall**.
3. With **lower aggregate demand**, the pressure on **prices eases**.

questions.stem_md:
Factories in an imagined economy are running below capacity and banks have plenty of deposits but lend little.

(a) Explain four quantitative instruments the central bank could use, stating the direction of each. [4]
(b) Why might these steps work only slowly? [1]
questions.solution_md: Four expansionary tools; limitation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) 1. **Cut the repo rate** and **bank rate**: banks get funds more cheaply and **lower loan rates**. 2. **Cut the CRR**: less cash must be kept with the central bank, so more can be **lent**. 3. **Cut the SLR**: fewer funds are tied up in approved securities. 4. **Buy government securities** in open market operations: **bank reserves rise** and credit becomes easier (a **lower reverse repo rate** also discourages parking funds with the central bank).
(b) Cheaper credit helps only if **firms and households want to borrow**; when they expect **weak sales**, they may not, so the effect is **slow**.

questions.stem_md: The governor of the imagined Swarnapur Central Bank meets the heads of banks and urges them, without any formal order, to go slow on loans for buying land. This method is

options.text_md: moral suasion
direct action
open market operations
raising the cash reserve ratio

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** moral suasion. Persuading banks through advice, letters and meetings, without legal compulsion, is moral suasion.

questions.stem_md: An imagined bank in Patna keeps lending for speculation despite repeated warnings. The central bank refuses it further rediscounting facilities and imposes a penalty. This is

options.text_md: moral suasion
a cut in the repo rate
credit rationing for all banks
direct action

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** direct action. Punitive steps against a particular bank that ignores the central bank's directions are direct action.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Swarnapur Central Bank fixes a ceiling on the total loans that banks may give for buying luxury cars. This qualitative tool is

options.text_md: the statutory liquidity ratio
credit rationing
the bank rate
a cash reserve ratio

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** credit rationing. Fixing ceilings or quotas on credit for particular purposes is credit rationing, a selective tool that controls the direction of credit.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Moral suasion has no legal force behind it.

**Reason (R):** Qualitative methods of credit control aim to influence the use or direction of credit rather than its total volume.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A: moral suasion lacks legal force because it is persuasion, not a rule; R describes qualitative methods in general.

questions.stem_md: True or false? If the imagined Swarnapur Central Bank raises the margin on loans against stocks of pulses from 30 to 50 per cent, a trader offering pulses worth ₹10 lakh as security can borrow less than before.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The trader could borrow ₹7 lakh with a 30 per cent margin but only ₹5 lakh with a 50 per cent margin, so hoarding with borrowed money becomes harder.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between quantitative and qualitative methods of credit control, with one example of each, for an imagined banking-awareness quiz in Thrissur.
questions.solution_md: Volume versus direction, each with an example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Quantitative** methods regulate the **total volume** of credit in the economy, for example the **CRR** or the **repo rate**. **Qualitative** (selective) methods regulate the **direction or use** of credit for particular purposes, for example **margin requirements** or credit rationing.

questions.stem_md: Traders in the imagined Swarnapur economy are borrowing from banks to hoard pulses, and pulse prices are rising, although other prices are steady. Suggest three qualitative steps for its central bank and explain why such steps suit this problem better than a general rise in the CRR.
questions.solution_md: Margin, rationing, moral suasion or direct action; targeted versus general.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Raise the margin** on loans against stocks of pulses, so traders get **less credit** for hoarding.
2. **Ration credit**: fix a **ceiling** on bank loans to pulse traders.
3. **Moral suasion**, backed by **direct action** against banks that ignore it. These steps target **one use of credit**; a higher CRR would cut credit to **every** borrower, hurting farmers and firms whose prices are steady.

marking_scheme.step: Why targeted beats a general CRR rise

questions.stem_md:
An imagined central bank faces rapid price rises in gold and land, fuelled by bank loans, while prices of everyday goods are stable.

(a) Explain four qualitative instruments it could use. [4]
(b) Evaluate one limitation of these instruments. [1]
questions.solution_md: Four qualitative tools and a limitation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) 1. **Margin requirements**: raise the margin on loans against **gold and land**, so less can be borrowed against them. 2. **Credit rationing**: fix **ceilings** on bank loans for buying gold or land. 3. **Moral suasion**: the governor **advises and persuades** banks, through letters and meetings, to curb such lending. 4. **Direct action**: **penalise** or deny facilities to banks that keep lending for speculation.
(b) Borrowers may **divert** loans taken for other purposes, or use **non-bank lenders**, so selective controls can be **evaded**; moral suasion also has **no legal force**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about an imagined cooperative's deposit of ₹50,000 in Vasundhara Bank, where the reserve ratio is 20 per cent. [2 + 2]

(i) Calculate the total deposits and the credit created by the banking system.
(ii) Explain why the actual amount may be smaller than your answer.
questions.solution_md: Multiplier arithmetic; leakages.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Credit multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.2 = **5**. Total deposits = 50,000 × 5 = **₹2,50,000**. Credit created = 2,50,000 − 50,000 = **₹2,00,000**.
(ii) The calculation assumes every loan comes back as a deposit. In practice some borrowers **keep cash** (a cash drain), banks may hold **extra reserves**, and there may not be enough **willing, creditworthy borrowers**, so each round is smaller and the total falls short.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [2 + 2]

(i) Explain how the RBI acts as a bankers' bank for the imagined commercial banks of Gujarat.
(ii) Explain how it acts as custodian of the country's foreign exchange reserves.
questions.solution_md: Bankers' bank; custodian.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Commercial banks keep part of their **reserves with the RBI**, **settle their claims** on one another through their accounts with it, and can **borrow from it** when short of funds, so it does for banks what they do for the public.
(ii) The RBI **holds the country's foreign currencies and gold**, manages them, and **buys or sells foreign currency** to smooth sharp swings in the **rupee's exchange rate** and to meet external payments.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Uses them to steady the rupee

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Primary deposits in the imagined Swarnapur economy are ₹1000 crore. Calculate the total deposits that banks can create with reserve ratios of 10 and 12.5 per cent, and explain the process behind the multiple.
(ii) Explain how the repo rate and open market operations could be used to support the change in (i) if the aim is to curb inflation.
questions.solution_md: Totals at two ratios and process; two supporting tools.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) With **10 per cent**, the multiplier is 10 and total deposits are **₹10,000 crore**; with **12.5 per cent**, it is 8 and deposits are **₹8,000 crore**, ₹2,000 crore less. **Process**: each bank keeps the required share of a deposit and **lends the rest**; the loan is spent and **redeposited** in another bank, which again keeps a reserve and lends; the rounds shrink, and their sum is the deposit divided by the reserve ratio. A higher ratio makes each round smaller.
(ii) **Raise the repo rate**: banks pay more for short-term funds from the central bank, so they **raise loan rates** and borrowing falls. **Sell government securities**: buyers pay out of bank deposits, so **bank reserves fall** and banks can lend less. Together with the higher reserve ratio, these steps make credit **dearer and scarcer**, cutting spending and easing **inflation**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Explain four functions of the Reserve Bank of India that make it the apex of the banking system.
(ii) Compare quantitative and qualitative methods of credit control, and judge which suits a price rise confined to a few commodities.
questions.solution_md: Four functions; comparison and judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) 1. **Bank of issue**: sole issuer of currency notes (except one-rupee notes). 2. **Banker to the government**: keeps its accounts and **manages its debt**. 3. **Bankers' bank and supervisor**: holds banks' reserves, clears their claims and regulates them. 4. **Lender of last resort**: rescues sound banks in a crisis (it is also custodian of foreign exchange).
(ii) **Quantitative** tools (repo and bank rate, CRR, SLR, open market operations) change the **total volume and cost** of credit for **everyone**. **Qualitative** tools (margins, credit rationing, moral suasion, direct action) steer the **direction** of credit for **particular uses**. When prices rise in only **a few commodities**, qualitative tools suit better: they curb **loans for hoarding those goods** without squeezing credit for the rest of the economy, though they can be **evaded** and are best backed by quantitative tightening if the rise spreads.

questions.stem_md: Study the imagined record of deposit creation that starts at Vasundhara Bank and answer the questions that follow. *(Written by SOYL for practice; the bank and figures are imagined.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Round 4 deposit = loan of round 3 = 25600, that is ₹25,600.

**(b)** Total deposits = 50,000 ÷ 0.2 = 250000, that is ₹2,50,000.

**(c) (i)** Reserves = r × total deposits = D.

**OR (c) (ii)** Cash drain lowers the total.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **₹25,600**

**(b)** **₹2,50,000**

**(c) (i)** Total reserves = 20 per cent of total deposits = 0.2 × 2,50,000 = **₹50,000**, exactly the **initial deposit**. Lending stops only when the whole of the new cash has been **absorbed as required reserves** across the banks.

**OR (c) (ii)** It is **not fully realistic**. Where people **hold cash**, part of each loan **does not return** as a deposit, so later rounds shrink faster and total deposits stay **below ₹2,50,000**.

questions.passage_md:
**Deposit creation after a weavers' cooperative deposits ₹50,000 (imagined; reserve ratio 20 per cent)**

| Round | Deposit (₹) | Reserve kept (₹) | Loan given (₹) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50,000 | 10,000 | 40,000 |
| 2 | 40,000 | 8,000 | 32,000 |
| 3 | 32,000 | 6,400 | 25,600 |

The bank manager says the process will continue through many more banks until no more can be lent.

children.stem_md: What will the deposit be in round 4 (in ₹)?
children.solution_md: Round 4 deposit = loan of round 3 = 25600, that is ₹25,600.

children.stem_md: Calculate the total deposits when the process is complete (in ₹).
**Either** (i): Show that, when the process is complete, total reserves equal the initial deposit, and explain why.

answer.model_answer_md: Total reserves = 20 per cent of total deposits = 0.2 × 2,50,000 = **₹50,000**, exactly the **initial deposit**. Lending stops only when the whole of the new cash has been **absorbed as required reserves** across the banks.

marking_scheme.step: Reason: process ends when cash is all held as reserves

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): The manager expects the full total. Comment on whether this is realistic in a rural district where people prefer to hold cash.

answer.model_answer_md: It is **not fully realistic**. Where people **hold cash**, part of each loan **does not return** as a deposit, so later rounds shrink faster and total deposits stay **below ₹2,50,000**.

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined minutes of a central bank meeting and answer the questions that follow. *(Written by SOYL for practice; the economy and figures are imagined.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Every step is contractionary.

**(b)** Margin and persuasion.

**(c) (i)** Reserves down, credit down, demand down.

**OR (c) (ii)** Broad plus targeted.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** To **contract** credit: it **raised the repo rate** (or the CRR, or sold securities).

**(b)** **Margin requirements** (on gold loans) and **moral suasion** (the meeting with bank chiefs).

**(c) (i)** Buyers pay for the securities from their **bank deposits**, so **bank reserves fall**. Banks must **cut lending**, credit becomes scarcer, **spending falls**, and the pressure on prices **eases**.

**OR (c) (ii)** General tools (repo, CRR, securities) cool **overall** demand, but by themselves they would squeeze **all borrowers**. Selective tools aim at **gold and land loans**, where the price rise is led. Together they curb the **source** of the rise while limiting harm to other sectors.

questions.passage_md:
**Minutes of the monetary committee, Swarnapur Central Bank (imagined)**

Prices have risen steadily for six months, led by gold and urban land, where buyers rely on bank loans. The committee decided to raise the policy repo rate, to raise the cash reserve ratio by half a percentage point, and to sell government securities worth a large amount over the next month. It also raised the margin on loans against gold and asked bank chiefs, at a meeting, to slow lending for land purchases.

children.stem_md: Is the central bank trying to expand or to contract credit? Give one piece of evidence.

answer.model_answer_md: To **contract** credit: it **raised the repo rate** (or the CRR, or sold securities).

children.stem_md: Name the qualitative methods mentioned in the minutes.

answer.model_answer_md: **Margin requirements** (on gold loans) and **moral suasion** (the meeting with bank chiefs).

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Explain how selling government securities will help to slow the price rise.
children.solution_md: Reserves down, credit down, demand down.

answer.model_answer_md: Buyers pay for the securities from their **bank deposits**, so **bank reserves fall**. Banks must **cut lending**, credit becomes scarcer, **spending falls**, and the pressure on prices **eases**.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Evaluate why the committee combined general and selective tools.

answer.model_answer_md: General tools (repo, CRR, securities) cool **overall** demand, but by themselves they would squeeze **all borrowers**. Selective tools aim at **gold and land loans**, where the price rise is led. Together they curb the **source** of the rise while limiting harm to other sectors.

marking_scheme.step: Role of selective tools and judgement

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined report on a new bank branch and answer the questions that follow. *(Written by SOYL for practice; the village and bank are imagined.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Deposits or loans.

**(b)** Agency.

**(c) (i)** Cash drain.

**OR (c) (ii)** Safe savings and cheaper credit.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Accepting deposits** (savings and recurring deposits), or **advancing loans** (crop loans, cash credit).

**(b)** An **agency function**: the bank acts as the farmers' **agent**.

**(c) (i)** Cash kept at home **does not come back** as deposits, so the branch and other banks receive **smaller new deposits** in later rounds. This **cash drain** keeps credit creation **well below** the multiplier formula.

**OR (c) (ii)** Families now earn **interest on safe deposits** instead of keeping cash in boxes, and they borrow at **lower, regulated rates** for crops and the dairy, so **production can expand** without heavy debt to the moneylender.

questions.passage_md:
**A year of the new branch in Hirapur village (imagined)**

Before the branch opened, families kept their savings in tin boxes and borrowed from a moneylender at very high interest. In its first year the branch opened savings and recurring-deposit accounts for 800 families, gave crop loans and a cash-credit limit to the village dairy, collected cheques for traders and paid farmers' insurance premiums on their instructions. Many families still withdraw loans in cash and keep it at home.

children.stem_md: Identify one primary function performed by the branch.

answer.model_answer_md: **Accepting deposits** (savings and recurring deposits), or **advancing loans** (crop loans, cash credit).

children.stem_md: Which kind of function is paying farmers' insurance premiums on their instructions?

answer.model_answer_md: An **agency function**: the bank acts as the farmers' **agent**.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Explain how the families' habit of keeping loans in cash affects the branch's ability to create credit.

answer.model_answer_md: Cash kept at home **does not come back** as deposits, so the branch and other banks receive **smaller new deposits** in later rounds. This **cash drain** keeps credit creation **well below** the multiplier formula.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Comment on how the branch has helped the village compared with the moneylender.

answer.model_answer_md: Families now earn **interest on safe deposits** instead of keeping cash in boxes, and they borrow at **lower, regulated rates** for crops and the dairy, so **production can expand** without heavy debt to the moneylender.
